headline: Broadcasters face financial instability and regulatory shifts across the Atlantic

digest.headline: Broadcasters face financial instability and regulatory shifts across the Atlantic
digest.lead: The BBC faces an existential crisis as cash reserves hit a decade low, while North American regulators approve major media mergers and recapitalisations. These developments coincide with significant legal challenges and technological shifts impacting the broadcasting landscapes in the United Kingdom, the United States and Canada.

glance.text: The BBC's cash reserves have dropped by 66 per cent in a single year to their lowest level in a decade.
Meta has launched a legal challenge against Ofcom over the implementation of the UK's Online Safety Act.
Channel 4 Sales has signed a deal to represent Channel 5 advertising, prompting calls for market scrutiny.
Ofcom has proposed new rules for smart speakers to protect radio station access, stream choices and advertising.
The House of Lords Communications and Digital Committee has laid out recommendations for the future BBC Charter.
News UK's Octave has launched direct sales of audio ads around its content on YouTube, including talkSPORT.
The FCC approved a 49.5 percent foreign equity stake in the merged Paramount-Warner Bros. entity.
The CRTC approved the transfer of Corus Entertainment's broadcasting licences to a new lender-controlled parent company.
Nielsen has halved its streaming ratings reporting delay, publishing weekly top-10 charts in 11 days instead of four weeks.
Disney has appointed former Meta and Microsoft executive Karandeep Anand as its first chief technology officer.
Google, Nvidia, Anthropic and Emerald AI have formed a coalition to secure 100 gigawatts of grid capacity for data centres.
Unsealed court documents reveal Microsoft and OpenAI executives previously described web scraping for AI training as a massive theft of labour.
Security researchers successfully used Anthropic's Claude AI assistant to breach OpenAI's internal code repository.

paragraphs: The BBC has spent hundreds of millions of pounds of its cash reserves in a single year, leaving its reserves at their lowest level in a decade. This drop of 66 per cent comes as the broadcaster undertakes deep cuts to save 500 million pounds.

Industry insiders warn that British public service broadcasters face a fight for survival against US giants like YouTube and Netflix. Jobs and programme budgets are in the firing line across the BBC, ITV and Channel 4.

Meta has launched a legal challenge against media regulator Ofcom over the implementation of the Online Safety Act. Critics accuse social media companies of using courts to slow down the new safety rules.
Ofcom has also proposed new rules for smart speakers to protect radio stations. The proposals aim to secure station access, stream choices and advertising when listeners use voice assistants.

Additionally, the House of Lords Communications and Digital Committee has written to the government with recommendations for the next BBC Charter. Separately, peers have proposed a ban on gambling advertisements.
Channel 4 Sales has secured a deal to represent Channel 5 advertising. Meanwhile, Channel 4's chief commercial officer has urged robust scrutiny over the implications of the Sky-ITV deal.
In sports rights, the BBC has signed a three-year agreement to broadcast the FIA World Rally Championship. The deal will bring live coverage of every round to UK audiences from 2027 to 2029.

The US Federal Communications Commission has waived its usual 25 percent limit on foreign equity ownership for the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger. The decision allows three Middle Eastern sovereign wealth funds from Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Abu Dhabi to own 49.5 percent of the non-voting equity in the combined company. Critics, including Senator Elizabeth Warren, have strongly condemned the decision and urged state attorneys general not to settle their antitrust lawsuits against the merger.

Meanwhile, Paramount is in advanced talks with California Attorney General Rob Bonta to settle the state-level antitrust challenge. To push the deal through, Paramount chief executive David Ellison has threatened to move the company's headquarters out of California, with the firm already scouting for office space in Nashville. Compromise proposals include operating the two movie studios separately for a set period.

In Canada, the CRTC has approved a major debt-for-equity recapitalisation plan for Corus Entertainment. The regulator approved the transfer of Corus's broadcasting licences to a new parent company, NewCo, which will be 99 percent owned by its lenders. The commission fast-tracked the decision to prevent further financial distress and secure the continuation of Corus's news services.

Nielsen has overhauled its streaming audience measurement system to deliver data much faster. The measurement firm has cut its reporting lag from four weeks down to just 11 days. The newly accelerated weekly top-10 charts saw Reacher take the top spot, with Lanterns also making its debut on the list.

NBC is also shaking up its distribution strategy by simulcasting the live shows of the upcoming season of The Voice on Peacock. This marks the first time the long-running music competition series will stream live on the platform alongside its traditional broadcast.

A new tech coalition comprising Google, Nvidia, Anthropic and Emerald AI is lobbying to find 100 gigawatts of power grid capacity. The group wants to speed up grid connections for new artificial intelligence data centres in exchange for offering energy flexibility. OpenAI is also looking at expansion, with its managing director calling Canada an obvious location for future data centres.

Newly unsealed court documents from the New York Times lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft have revealed internal anxieties over data scraping. Documents show that Microsoft and OpenAI executives privately worried about a web doom loop. One executive even described their scraping of publisher data as the largest theft of labour in human history.
